AUDUSD is the biggest mover of the major currencies this week.  The price falls -2.30% for the week.
body: The AUDUSD is the weakest of the major currencies vs the greenback. It fell -2.3%. The price has now fallen for 10 consecutive days. That move has taken the price from a high on November 10 at 0.69296 to the low today at 0.6609 or -320 pips.

The 320-pip slide in AUDUSD started with a repricing of Fed rate expectations and picked up steam as Australia’s jobs market weakened and the global equity selloff deepened. The Aussie’s 2.30% decline this week, the largest of the seven majors you tracked against the USD, also reflected weakness against other currencies, including the yen and euro.

On the daily chart, AUDUSD broke below 0.6751 earlier this week, taking out the 38.2% retracement of the rally from the 2025 low. Sellers kept the pressure on, pushing through swing levels at 0.6706 and 0.66588 in succession.

The next downside target is 0.65905, the 50% retracement of that same rally. On a rebound, 0.66588 is the first barometer for buyers. Getting back above that level would take some of the pressure off.

Drilling down to the hourly chart, the AUDUSD selloff started on November 2 with a break below the 100- and 200-hour moving averages. The pair corrected higher on November 4, but by November 5 it was back below both averages. The price has stayed below the lower 100-hour MA ever since.

That 100-hour MA now comes in at 0.67017 and is the first barometer for buyers. They need to get and stay above it to begin to wrestle back some control. If they can do that, the next target is 0.6730, the 38.2% retracement of the move down from the November 9 high. Above that, the 200-hour MA at 0.67586 is the next hurdle.
Until buyers can get and stay above 0.67017, the sellers remain in control on the hourly chart

news.title: Peterson: The Fed's chairman sees an AI revolution coming. Now he has to figure out what it means
body: Artificial intelligence is about to sweep through the economy. The Federal Reserve is bracing for impact.

"We are at a hinge point in the U.S. economy," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said at a conference he convened in San Francisco on Monday. But exactly when and how the economy could turn, and what that means for interest rates and inflation, isn't yet clear.

The meeting of Warsh's AI task force saw the new Fed chairman publicly asking the questions Americans will ultimately expect him to answer. He hinted at a few of his private views on whether white-collar workers could soon face massive job losses, but he largely left the speculation to an array of experts he has assembled to advise the Fed.

With the technology racing ahead, Warsh won't be able to put off giving his own answers much longer. AI lab Anthropic plans to price the shares for its initial public offering on Wednesday and could raise as much as $64 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation. Vast spending from AI firms is prompting the Fed to contemplate raising interest rates in December to slow down the rate of price increases as the tech sector heats up the economy.

Meanwhile Americans are souring on some aspects of the technology. The Nov. 3 midterms saw voters enact an array of state-level measures to slow down construction of the data centers that are essential to powering AI.

Warsh moderated three out of four sessions at Monday's event and was involved in selecting the speakers. Among them was one of the few prominent Democrats who was willing to speak out against that anti-data center trend.

It is "a very troubling sign" that so many anti-data center measures passed in the midterms, Gina Raimondo said. She is a former secretary of Commerce under President Joe Biden and a former governor of Rhode Island.
Stopping AI "would be very bad for America" and for the people who voted for the measures, Raimondo said.
Warsh didn't say whether he shares that view, and how it would translate into monetary policy isn't exactly clear.

The event was an unusual one for the Fed. The central bank employs a small army of Ph.D. economists who can rapidly weigh in on anything affecting the U.S. and global economies. But in keeping with his long-standing critiques of the Fed as insular and outdated, Warsh has chosen to draw expertise from outside the institution to help it figure out how to think about what AI will do to productivity and jobs.
Warsh has assembled a task force on that issue, alongside four others devoted to aspects of Fed policymaking.

The public heard Monday from one of the three official members of the task force: venture capitalist Marc Andreessen. Warsh went to Stanford University with Andreessen's wife, and the two have been longtime friends. Another task force member, Stanford economist Chad Jones, is on leave and working at Anthropic and couldn't speak during the company's blackout period ahead of the IPO. The third, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, didn't attend the event.

Andreessen is hugely optimistic about the promise of AI as a technology, but believes the government won't let Americans experience its full effects. Heavy regulation in areas such as healthcare and education mean technology can't replace people's jobs in those sectors, he said.

"To the extent our economy is a free market economy, then maybe you could see the, let's say, extremely rapid displacement scenarios people are talking about," Andreessen said. "But we've mostly outlawed the kind of job transition that … both the utopians the doomers talk about."

news.title: Trump weighs renewed strikes on Iran as military warns of strain. FT
body: President Donald Trump is considering new strikes on Iran, the Financial Times reports, as hawkish officials in Washington and Israel urge him to resume military action.

U.S. military planners are warning that American forces risk becoming overextended if the standoff drags into the new year. The warning adds pressure on Trump as he weighs whether to restart strikes and how long U.S. forces can sustain their current posture.

For markets, crude oil is the first place to watch. The report puts escalation risk back in focus, and the next question for traders is whether that risk starts to translate into a bigger premium for potential supply disruptions.

...and there are strains on the world because back on February 28, a war was started with what was thought would be a quick end, but which has proved not be quick at all and the implications are contributing to strains everywhere.
The good news is it took 15 hours to get back to Washington from China, and the President saw his friends.

news.title: Fed’s Cook says monetary policy isn’t restrictive enough
body: The Fed’s Cook weighed in on inflation, the labor market and the need for tighter monetary policy in remarks that crossed the wires.

These are hawkish comments from Cook. In her view, the September hike didn’t deliver enough restraint, and financial conditions are still too easy. With growth strong and the labor market holding up, she sees room for the Fed to tighten further. She also says tariffs’ impact on inflation has faded, yet the current level of inflation remains a concern.

For traders, the strongest policy signal is how Cook frames the cost of waiting. If inflation becomes embedded, she thinks the Fed will have to respond more aggressively. That puts more weight on the next inflation readings and whether they give the Fed any room to hold rates steady.

Let's face it, the Fed kept rates unchanged at the October meeting. The minutes suggested a more hawkish bias. The election likely was influence. The Fed officials seem to suggest that inflation is not getting better but worse.

Meanwhile the US yields are moving lower with the shorter end of the yield curve down -14 basis points at 4.64%. The 10 year is down -11.62 basis points at 4.935%. For the 2 year, the low yield in November reached 4.448%. So the yield is still well above that level. As far as Fed expectations, in December the chance for remaining unchanged actually increased to 4.2%. The chance for a 50 basis point hike is now 0% while the chance of a 25 basis point hike is 95.8%.
Stocks continue to get hammered with the NASDAQ composite down -3.51% in the NASDAQ 100 down -3.76%.
